Bringing Order to Asynchronous SGD: Towards Optimality under Data-Dependent Delays with Momentum

Tehila Dahan∗ Affiliation: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology, Haifa, Israel    Roie Reshef∗ Affiliation: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology, Haifa, Israel    Sharon Goldstein Affiliation: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology, Haifa, Israel    Kfir Y. Levy Affiliation: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology, Haifa, Israel
Abstract

Asynchronous stochastic gradient descent (SGD) enables scalable distributed training but suffers from gradient staleness. Existing mitigation strategies, such as delay-adaptive learning rates and staleness-aware filtering, typically attenuate or discard delayed gradients, introducing systematic bias: updates from simpler or faster-to-process samples are overrepresented, while gradients from more complex samples are delayed or suppressed. In contrast, prior approaches to data-dependent delays rely on a Lipschitz assumption that yields suboptimal rates or leave the smooth, convex case unaddressed. We propose a momentum-based asynchronous framework designed to preserve information from delayed gradients while mitigating the effects of staleness. We establish the first optimal convergence rates for data-dependent delays in both convex and non-convex smooth setups, providing a new result for asynchronous optimization under standard assumptions. Additionally, we derive robust learning-rate schedules that simplify hyperparameter tuning in practice.

1 Introduction

The rapid growth of dataset sizes and model complexity has made distributed training indispensable in modern machine learning (Verbraeken et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2023). Among existing scaling strategies, asynchronous parallelization is particularly appealing, as it reduces synchronization overhead and improves resource utilization (Mishchenko et al., 2022). In this setting, multiple workers independently compute gradients on different mini-batches and update shared model parameters without requiring global synchronization. This design offers several advantages, including reduced communication costs, elimination of idle time caused by stragglers, and efficient utilization of heterogeneous hardware. In contrast to synchronous methods, which require all workers to wait for the slowest one before proceeding to the next update (Dekel et al., 2012), asynchronous SGD enables continuous updates, yielding higher throughput in wall-clock time and making it well-suited for scalable learning. These advantages, however, come at a fundamental cost: updates may be delayed and thus stale. Specifically, by the time a worker applies its computed gradient, the global model may have already evolved, resulting in a discrepancy commonly referred to as staleness.

Tight analyses of arbitrary delays typically rely on the assumption that staleness is independent of the data (Cohen et al., 2021; Attia et al., 2024; Aviv et al., 2021; Mishchenko et al., 2022; Koloskova et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2024). In modern training procedures, delays are inherently data-dependent; the computation time of a mini-batch often scales with the input complexity. For instance, in language modeling, to maximize hardware efficiency, sequences are often bucketed by length (Guo et al., 2025; Pouransari et al., 2024), causing batches with longer, more complex sequences to experience significantly higher staleness due to the superlinear scaling of self-attention (Vaswani et al., 2017). An analogous phenomenon arises in video understanding, where longer clips impose heavier computational loads. This coupling between the data distribution and delay biases the optimization process toward easy examples, leading to instability, slower convergence, and degraded generalization.

To mitigate this effect, recent data-dependent analyses scale the learning rate with the number of workers MM (Mishchenko et al., 2022; Koloskova et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2024). However, these results remain suboptimal for general LL-smooth objectives. Specifically, in non-convex settings, they rely on a GG-Lipschitz (bounded gradient) assumption that introduces an additional suboptimal term in the convergence rate. Furthermore, in the smooth-convex setting, a result on data-dependent delays is currently absent from the literature.

More specifically, in the non-convex setting, existing data-dependent analyses (Mishchenko et al., 2022) yield the rate

𝒪⁡(L​Δ​MT+σ​L​ΔT+(G​L​Δ​MT)2/3)\displaystyle\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{L\Delta M}{T}+\frac{\sigma\sqrt{L\Delta}}{\sqrt{T}}+\left(\frac{GL\Delta M}{T}\right)^{2/3}\right) (1)

where Δ\Delta denotes the optimality gap and σ\sigma denoting the stochastic error. This rate contains an additional 𝒪⁡((G​L​Δ​MT)2/3)\mathcal{O}\left(\left(\frac{GL\Delta M}{T}\right)^{2/3}\right) term that is suboptimal and arises from the bounded-gradient assumption.

In the convex case, existing data-dependent analyses (Mishchenko et al., 2022) yield the rate

𝒪⁡(G​D​MT)\displaystyle\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{GD\sqrt{M}}{\sqrt{T}}\right) (2)

where DD bounds the distance between two feasible points. This result is limited by its reliance on a GG-Lipschitz assumption and does not leverage the objective’s smoothness. Under standard smoothness assumptions, the well-known data-independent rate is 𝒪⁡(L​D2​MT+σ​DT)\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{LD^{2}M}{T}+\frac{\sigma D}{\sqrt{T}}\right). A critical discrepancy emerges here: in the smooth case, the dominant 𝒪⁡(1T)\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\right) term is independent of the number of workers MM, whereas the existing data-dependent rate incurs a M\sqrt{M} penalty. Unfortunately, a result that recovers this MM-independent dominant term while accounting for data-dependent delays is currently absent from the literature.

From the standpoint of parallelization, these bounds fail to capture the acceleration potential of using many workers. In the non-convex setting, the rate remains disproportionately large relative to the stochastic noise, stifling the attainable speedup (see Remark 4.2). The discrepancy is even more severe in the convex case, where the M\sqrt{M} factor is on the dominant, slow 𝒪⁡(1T)\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\right) term. Closing these gaps in a fully data-dependent and smooth setting remains an open challenge that we address in this work.

Under data-independent assumptions, several existing approaches mitigate the effect of delays by filtering updates based on their staleness. In particular, some methods adjust the learning rate as a function of the observed delay (Mishchenko et al., 2022; Koloskova et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2024; Venigalla et al., 2020; Barkai et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2022), while others employ delay-based filtering thresholds that directly discard excessively stale updates (Cohen et al., 2021; Attia et al., 2024; Maranjyan et al., 2025). These techniques downweight delayed gradients and thereby reinforce the bias toward samples that are processed quickly. Moreover, these methods introduce additional hyperparameters that may be difficult to tune. For example, Mishchenko et al. (2022); Koloskova et al. (2022); Shi et al. (2024) show that for smooth objectives without Lipschitz continuity, the optimal learning rate is

ηt=min⁡{Θ⁡(1L​τt),Θ⁡(1L​M),Θ⁡(ΔL​σ2​T)}\displaystyle\eta_{t}=\min\left\{\Theta\left(\frac{1}{L\tau_{t}}\right),\Theta\left(\frac{1}{LM}\right),\Theta\left(\sqrt{\frac{\Delta}{L\sigma^{2}T}}\right)\right\} (3)

which depends on the smoothness constant LL, the current delay τt\tau_{t}, the optimality gap Δ\Delta, and the stochastic error σ\sigma. Since most of these quantities are generally unknown in practice, it is less practical to evaluate ηt\eta_{t} at each iteration. In contrast to a fixed learning rate, which can be tuned once using simple and standard strategies such as a grid search (Liashchynskyi and Liashchynskyi, 2019), these adaptive schedules require continual approximation, making asynchronous training more delicate and tuning-intensive.

Our Contributions

In this work, we propose a momentum-based framework that resolves the suboptimality induced by data-dependent delays in asynchronous learning. Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We provide the first optimal convergence rates for asynchronous learning under data-dependent delays in both convex and non-convex smooth settings:

    1. 1.

      In the smooth non-convex case, prior data-dependent work additionally assumed that the gradients are GG-bounded, and the rate is suboptimal by having an additional 𝒪⁡((G​L​Δ​MT)2/3)\mathcal{O}\left(\left(\frac{GL\Delta M}{T}\right)^{2/3}\right) term, implying degraded parallelization compared to the optimal (data-independent) bound.

    2. 2.

      In the convex case, optimal results for the smooth case are non-existent. But under a GG-bounded gradient assumption, the rate is 𝒪⁡(G​MT)\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{G\sqrt{M}}{\sqrt{T}}\right). Unfortunately, the leading term in this bound degrades as the number of machines MM increases, implying degraded performance upon parallelization. Conversely, our new results for the smooth data-dependent case analysis imply that the leading term does not depend on MM, a nontrivial benefit of parallelization (as is common in smooth-case analysis).

  • •

    Our guarantees hold with a fixed learning rate that can be optimized once via standard offline procedures, such as a single grid search. In contrast, existing delay-adaptive methods require per-iteration step sizes of the form ηt=min⁡{Θ⁡(1L​τt),Θ⁡(1L​M),Θ⁡(ΔL​σ2​T)}\eta_{t}=\min\left\{\Theta\left(\frac{1}{L\tau_{t}}\right),\Theta\left(\frac{1}{LM}\right),\Theta\left(\sqrt{\frac{\Delta}{L\sigma^{2}T}}\right)\right\}. Because this schedule depends on unobservable quantities, it must be re-evaluated at every iteration rather than tuned once globally. In the convex setting, we leverage a double-momentum mechanism that ensures stable convergence over a broad range of learning rates, further reducing hyperparameter sensitivity and enhancing stability in such noisy asynchronous setups.

2 Related Work

Asynchronous SGD has long been studied as a means to scale optimization across multiple workers by eliminating synchronization barriers (Tsitsiklis et al., 2003; Mishchenko et al., 2022). Early analyses typically focused on the fixed-delay setting (Arjevani et al., 2020; Stich and Karimireddy, 2020; Zheng et al., 2017; Giladi et al., 2019), where every update has the same staleness. While this abstraction provides clean guarantees and remains relevant for homogeneous resources, it fails to capture the variability inherent in many practical scenarios, such as training across heterogeneous clusters or edge devices. To model such settings, other works introduced the bounded-delay assumption with a delay bound τmax\tau_{\max} (Stich et al., 2021; Lian et al., 2015; Agarwal and Duchi, 2011; Recht et al., 2011; Mania et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2025; Feyzmahdavian et al., 2016; Leblond et al., 2018). However, convergence rates under this assumption degrade proportionally with τmax\tau_{\max}, which in practice may be very large, even on the order of the total number of iterations TT, leading to impractical guarantees.

To address these limitations, recent works introduced the idea of virtual iterates, first studied under bounded delays (Mania et al., 2017) and fixed delays (Stich and Karimireddy, 2020), and later extended to sharper analysis (Mishchenko et al., 2022; Koloskova et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2024). The key idea is to analyze the algorithm as if it were updating a delay-free sequence of virtual points, and then bound the discrepancy between these iterates and the actual asynchronous ones. This abstraction yields sharper guarantees, with convergence rates scaling in the number of workers MM rather than τmax\tau_{\max}. Nonetheless, existing results remain limited: some achieve only suboptimal rates in data-dependent settings and rely on bounded-gradient assumptions. Others employ delay-adaptive methods that adjust the learning rate, but this requires assuming delay–data independence (Aviv et al., 2021; Mishchenko et al., 2022; Koloskova et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2024). Another line of work filters stale updates (Cohen et al., 2021; Attia et al., 2024; Maranjyan et al., 2025), which also relies on the same independence assumption. Both adaptive and filtering strategies bias training toward easier samples either by downweighting or discarding harder ones, while wasting computation and potentially harming generalization.

Momentum methods are a cornerstone of optimization and widely used in modern machine learning systems (Polyak, 1964; Nesterov, 2013; Kingma and Ba, 2015; Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017). Early asynchronous momentum-based approaches focused on restrictive settings, such as bounded delays (Barkai et al., 2019; Hakimi et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2025) or fixed delays (Giladi et al., 2019), which limit their applicability in variable environments. More recently, Shi et al. (2024) introduced the concept of ideal momentum, which adds new gradients with a weight that corresponds to their weight in the synchronous setting. Their approach further aggregates updates into groups of size MM and applies a uniform weight within each group. Despite these advances, their convergence guarantees remain suboptimal under data-dependent delays and rely on bounded-gradient assumptions. In contrast, we introduce a refined notion of ideal momentum that, for the first time, achieves tight convergence guarantees under data-dependent delays using a simple, constant learning rate. To further mitigate sensitivity to learning-rate selection, we analyze the convex case through the double-momentum method (Dahan and Levy, 2025), showing that its hallmark stability is preserved: optimality remains robust across a wide range of learning rates, even in highly variable asynchronous environments.

3 Settings

We consider the minimization of a smooth objective ff:

f⁡(𝐱):=𝔼𝐳∼𝒟​[f⁡(𝐱,𝐳)]\displaystyle f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right):=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[f\!\left(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{z}\right)\right]

where 𝒟\mathcal{D} is an unknown data distribution from which we draw i.i.d. samples {𝐳t}t=1T\{\mathbf{z}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}. We focus on iterative first-order optimization methods that access stochastic gradients of ff to generate a sequence of iterates {𝐱t}t=1T\{\mathbf{x}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}.

We consider a distributed framework with MM workers coordinated by a central parameter server (𝒫​𝒮\mathcal{PS}). Each worker can compute a stochastic gradient oracle 𝐠∈d\mathbf{g}\in\real^{d}, defined as 𝐠:=∇f​(𝐱,𝐳)\mathbf{g}:=\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{z}\right) with 𝐳∼𝒟\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{D}. This oracle is unbiased in expectation, i.e., 𝔼​[𝐠∣𝐱]=∇f​(𝐱)\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{g}\mid\mathbf{x}\right]=\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right).

Our analysis considers the asynchronous optimization setting, in which the 𝒫​𝒮\mathcal{PS} updates the global model immediately upon receiving an update from any worker. Such asynchrony introduces delays and can destabilize the learning process, since gradients are computed using stale model parameters and may be applied out of order. We denote by τt≥0\tau_{t}\geq 0 the delay associated with the update applied at iteration tt. Importantly, the delay τt\tau_{t} may depend on the underlying data sample 𝐳t−τt\mathbf{z}_{t-\tau_{t}}, capturing realistic scenarios where computation or communication times vary across samples.

Asynchronous SGD.

In this asynchronous setting, the standard SGD update (Mishchenko et al., 2022; Koloskova et al., 2022) takes the form

𝐱t+1=𝐱t−ηt​𝐠t−τt\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\mathbf{x}_{t}-\eta_{t}\mathbf{g}_{t-\tau_{t}} (4)

where ηt>0\eta_{t}>0 is the learning rate and 𝐠t−τt:=∇f​(𝐱t−τt,𝐳t−τt)\mathbf{g}_{t-\tau_{t}}:=\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t-\tau_{t}};\mathbf{z}_{t-\tau_{t}}\right) denotes a stochastic gradient evaluated at a delayed iterate 𝐱t−τt\mathbf{x}_{t-\tau_{t}}.

Notations. Throughout the paper, ‖⋅‖\left\|\cdot\right\| denotes the Euclidean (ℓ2)(\ell_{2}) norm. For any N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, we define [N]:={1,…,N}[N]:=\{1,\ldots,N\}.

4 Momentum-Based Asynchronous Framework

Momentum has long been a cornerstone of optimization, valued for its ability to accelerate convergence and stabilize noisy updates in stochastic settings (Polyak, 1964; Nesterov, 2013; Kingma and Ba, 2015; Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017; Jordan et al., ). At a high level, momentum augments vanilla SGD by maintaining a running average of past gradients, thereby blending historical information with the current update direction. Formally, in the single-worker setting, the classical momentum method introduced by Polyak (1964) updates the momentum buffer and parameters as

𝐦tsyn=β​𝐠t+(1−β)​𝐦t−1syn,𝐱t+1=𝐱t−η​𝐦tsyn\displaystyle\mathbf{m}_{t}^{\text{syn}}=\beta\mathbf{g}_{t}+(1-\beta)\mathbf{m}_{t-1}^{\text{syn}},\quad\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\mathbf{x}_{t}-\eta\mathbf{m}_{t}^{\text{syn}} (5)

where η>0\eta>0 is the learning rate, β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) is the momentum parameter, 𝐠t:=∇f​(𝐱t,𝐳t)\mathbf{g}_{t}:=\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t};\mathbf{z}_{t}\right) is the stochastic gradient at step tt, and 𝐦tsyn\mathbf{m}_{t}^{\text{syn}} denotes the momentum buffer in the single-worker synchronous baseline.

4.1 Assumptions

We impose standard assumptions commonly used in the analysis of non-convex stochastic optimization:

Let f:d→f:\real^{d}\to\real be our objective function.

Lower Bounded Function Value: f∗:=inf𝐱∈d​f​(𝐱)>−∞.f^{*}:=\underset{\mathbf{x}\in\real^{d}}{\inf}f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)>-\infty. We will define Δ:=f⁡(𝐱1)−f∗\Delta:=f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{1}\right)-f^{*}.

Bounded Variance: There exists σ>0\sigma>0 such that ∀𝐱∈d\forall\mathbf{x}\in\real^{d}: 𝔼​‖∇f​(𝐱,𝐳)−∇f​(𝐱)‖2≤σ2\mathbb{E}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{z}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)\right\|^{2}\leq\sigma^{2}.

Smoothness: There exist L>0L>0 such that ∀𝐱,𝐲∈d\forall\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\real^{d}: ‖∇f​(𝐱)−∇f​(𝐲)‖≤L⁡‖𝐱−𝐲‖\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{y}\right)\right\|\leq L\left\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\right\|.

4.2 Momentum-Based Solution

A straightforward extension of the classical momentum method to the asynchronous setting is given by incorporating delayed stochastic gradients into the momentum recursion. Specifically, at iteration tt, let τt≥0\tau_{t}\geq 0 denote the delay associated with the stochastic gradient used at that iteration. The gradient 𝐠t−τt:=∇f​(𝐱t−τt,𝐳t−τt)\mathbf{g}_{t-\tau_{t}}:=\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t-\tau_{t}};\mathbf{z}_{t-\tau_{t}}\right) is evaluated at a past iterate 𝐱t−τt\mathbf{x}_{t-\tau_{t}}. The naive asynchronous momentum updates are then defined as

𝐦tasy=β​𝐠t−τt+(1−β)​𝐦t−1asy\displaystyle\mathbf{m}^{\text{asy}}_{t}=\beta\mathbf{g}_{t-\tau_{t}}+(1-\beta)\mathbf{m}^{\text{asy}}_{t-1} (6)

where 𝐦tasy\mathbf{m}^{\text{asy}}_{t} denotes the momentum buffer maintained under asynchronous updates. This formulation reduces to the classical single-worker momentum method when τt=0\tau_{t}=0 for all tt, in which case 𝐦tasy=𝐦tsyn\mathbf{m}^{\text{asy}}_{t}=\mathbf{m}_{t}^{\text{syn}}.

Despite its simplicity, this extension in Equation 6 introduces a fundamental challenge in asynchronous learning, as the momentum recursion can amplify the influence of gradients computed on more stale parameters compared to those computed on more recent ones.

More specifically, while momentum is usually expressed in its recursive form, this representation can obscure how past information contributes to the update. A useful perspective of Equation 5 comes from unrolling the recursion, which makes explicit the contribution of each past gradient. Expanding the update yields

𝐦tsyn=β​∑τ=0t−1(1−β)τ​𝐠t−τ\displaystyle\mathbf{m}_{t}^{\text{syn}}=\beta\sum_{\tau=0}^{t-1}(1-\beta)^{\tau}\mathbf{g}_{t-\tau} (7)

This expansion reveals that momentum is an exponential moving average over all past gradients. Thus, the gradient from τ\tau iterations ago is weighted by exactly β​(1−β)τ\beta(1-\beta)^{\tau}, where (1−β)τ(1-\beta)^{\tau} reflects its “distance” from the current iterate. In other words, momentum naturally emphasizes recent gradients while retaining a fading echo of older ones.

Our Proposal.

The explicit form of the momentum recursion in Equation 7 admits a clean and intuitive interpretation. In the ideal (delay-free) setting, each stochastic gradient contributes to the momentum buffer according to its exact position in an exponentially decaying sequence: a gradient computed τ\tau iterations in the past is weighted by β​(1−β)τ\beta(1-\beta)^{\tau}. Preserving this ideal ordering suggests that, under delays, each gradient should be incorporated using precisely the weight it would receive in the single-worker trajectory. Motivated by this observation, we modify the asynchronous momentum update to

𝐦t=β​(1−β)τt​𝐠t−τt+(1−β)​𝐦t−1\displaystyle\mathbf{m}_{t}=\beta(1-\beta)^{\tau_{t}}\mathbf{g}_{t-\tau_{t}}+(1-\beta)\mathbf{m}_{t-1} (8)

A related “ordered weighting” perspective was recently highlighted by Shi et al. (2024), who group iterations into blocks of size MM and assign each block a uniform weight in their virtual momentum construction that mimics the ideal momentum. In contrast, we adopt the same underlying principle but enforce it exactly. Specifically, each delayed gradient 𝐠t−τt\mathbf{g}_{t-\tau_{t}} is assigned the exact coefficient β​(1−β)τt\beta(1-\beta)^{\tau_{t}} it would have in the ideal, delay-free trajectory. As a result, stale gradients are neither discarded nor treated as fresh; instead, they are consistently integrated into the virtual momentum structure, with any deviation arising solely from missing future gradients that have not yet arrived.

Formally, for iteration t≥1t\geq 1 and index 1≤k≤t1\leq k\leq t, define the weighted gradient as

𝐠t,k:=β​(1−β)t−k​𝐠k\displaystyle\mathbf{g}_{t,k}:=\beta(1-\beta)^{t-k}\mathbf{g}_{k}

where, in the first step, we only use the contribution of the first worker, while the other workers replace the first gradient they receive with zero.

Thus, the resulting delayed momentum with ordered weights (Equations 8 and 1) can be represented as

𝐦t=∑k∈[t]/𝒯⁡(t)𝐠t,k\displaystyle\mathbf{m}_{t}=\sum_{k\in[t]/\mathcal{T}(t)}\mathbf{g}_{t,k} (9)

Where 𝒯⁡(t)\mathcal{T}(t) denotes the set of iteration indices whose gradients have not yet arrived by time tt, and therefore |𝒯⁡(t)|≤M−1|\mathcal{T}(t)|\leq M-1. Equation 9 collects all updates that have been computed on the model parameters up to iteration tt, ignoring all the gradients for the iterations that have not yet arrived and are therefore still missing. Consequently, the resulting ordered-momentum buffer incorporates only stochastic gradients that have arrived by iteration tt. The weighted ordering preserves the structure of the ideal momentum, with the only deviation being the subtraction of at most M−1M-1 pending gradients. With these definitions, we define the virtual momentum 𝐦^t\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{t} at iteration tt as

𝐦^t:=∑k∈[t]/𝒯⁡(t)𝐠t,k+∑k∈𝒯⁡(t)𝐠¯t,k\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{t}:=\sum_{k\in[t]/\mathcal{T}(t)}\mathbf{g}_{t,k}+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{T}(t)}\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t,k} (10)

where 𝐠¯t,k:=β(1−β)t−k∇f(𝐱t)\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t,k}:=\beta(1-\beta)^{t-k}\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right) represents the expected gradient used to fill in the missing iterations. We shall use these gradients only for the sake of analysis. Specifically, we shall use these gradients to define a virtual (impractical) version of the momentum, which serves as an analytical tool for comparing with and analyzing the practical momentum used in Algorithm 1.

Finally, the stochastic error of delayed momentum, ϵt:=𝐦t−∇f​(𝐱t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}:=\mathbf{m}_{t}-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right), can be decomposed as

ϵt=ϵ^t+𝐛t\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}+\mathbf{b}_{t}

where ϵ^t=𝐦^t−∇f​(𝐱t)\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}=\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{t}-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right) is the error of the virtual momentum and 𝐛t\mathbf{b}_{t} is the difference induced by delay. This difference has the explicit form

𝐛t\displaystyle\mathbf{b}_{t} :=𝐦t−𝐦^t=−∑k∈𝒯⁡(t)𝐠¯t,k\displaystyle:=\mathbf{m}_{t}-\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{t}=-\sum_{k\in\mathcal{T}(t)}\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t,k} (11)

which scales at most linearly with the number of workers, i.e., ‖𝐛t‖≤𝒪⁡(M)\left\|\mathbf{b}_{t}\right\|\leq\mathcal{O}\left(M\right). This leads to a stochastic error term for delayed momentum, ϵt\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}, whose bound is independent of per-sample delays. Instead, it depends only on (i) a factor in the number of workers MM, rather than the delay itself, and (ii) the same stochastic error present in the ideal (delay-free) case. The core intuition is that our asynchronous momentum aims to be as close as possible to ideal, delay-free momentum; consequently, the resulting bias is restricted to a transient 𝒪⁡(M)\mathcal{O}\left(M\right) term, accounting only for the future missing updates, rather than scaling with the magnitude of the delays.

Theorem 4.1 (Nonconvex Smooth Objectives).

Let ff satisfy the assumptions in Section 4.1. Consider the iterates {𝐱t}t=1T\{\mathbf{x}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} generated by Algorithm 1 with β=min⁡{116​(M−1),5​L​Δσ​T}\beta=\min\left\{\frac{1}{16(M-1)},\frac{\sqrt{5L\Delta}}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}\right\}, and η=min⁡{132​2​L​(M−1),5​Δ2​σ​2​L​T}\eta=\min\left\{\frac{1}{32\sqrt{2}L(M-1)},\frac{\sqrt{5\Delta}}{2\sigma\sqrt{2LT}}\right\}. Then

1T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖∇f​(𝐱t)‖2≤𝒪⁡(L​Δ​MT+σ​L​ΔT)\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\right\|^{2}\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{L\Delta M}{T}+\frac{\sigma\sqrt{L\Delta}}{\sqrt{T}}\right)
Remark 4.2.

Optimality under Data-Dependent Delays. When data independence is not assumed, existing analyses typically impose an additional bounded-gradient assumption, i.e., ‖∇f​(𝐱)‖≤G\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)\right\|\leq G for some G>0G>0 (Mishchenko et al., 2022; Koloskova et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2024). Under this assumption, the resulting convergence bounds (see Equation 1) incur an extra error term of order 𝒪⁡((G​L​Δ​MT)2/3)\mathcal{O}\left(\left(\frac{GL\Delta M}{T}\right)^{2/3}\right). To exploit parallelization across multiple workers, i.e., to ensure that this term does not dominate the stochastic error 𝒪⁡(1T)\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\right), it is necessary that (MT)2/3≤𝒪⁡(1T)\left(\frac{M}{T}\right)^{2/3}\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\right), which implies that these results permit parallelization only up to M≤𝒪⁡(T1/4)M\leq\mathcal{O}\left(T^{1/4}\right) workers without degrading the convergence rate. In contrast, our analysis avoids this additional slowdown term and does not rely on bounded-gradient assumptions. Consequently, our method supports parallelization up to the natural limit M=𝒪⁡(T)M=\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{T}\right) while preserving the optimal convergence rate, yielding sharper guarantees under weaker assumptions.

Remark 4.3.

Generality to Data-Dependent Delays. Our guarantees apply to general smooth nonconvex objectives without assuming independence between the delays and the data. In contrast, existing works that obtain comparable convergence guarantees rely on a delay–data independence assumption (Mishchenko et al., 2022; Koloskova et al., 2022; Cohen et al., 2021; Aviv et al., 2021; Maranjyan et al., 2025; Attia et al., 2024; Feyzmahdavian and Johansson, 2023; Wu et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2024). Such assumptions can be restrictive in practice, as delays are often data-dependent, with more complex or informative samples incurring longer computation times. By avoiding this assumption, our analysis aligns with standard assumptions for smooth objectives in state-of-the-art SGD theory (Dekel et al., 2012) and more faithfully captures the asynchronous dynamics in reality.

Remark 4.4.

Practical Learning Rate and Hyperparameter Tuning. Our guarantees hold with a fixed learning rate, which can be optimized via standard offline procedures such as a single grid search. In contrast, existing delay-adaptive methods (Mishchenko et al., 2022; Koloskova et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2024) require per-iteration step sizes of the form ηt=min⁡{Θ⁡(1L​τt),Θ⁡(1L​M),Θ⁡(ΔL​σ2​T)}\eta_{t}=\min\left\{\Theta\left(\frac{1}{L\tau_{t}}\right),\Theta\left(\frac{1}{LM}\right),\Theta\left(\sqrt{\frac{\Delta}{L\sigma^{2}T}}\right)\right\}. Because this schedule depends on unobservable, problem-specific quantities, such as the smoothness LL and the optimality gap Δ\Delta, it must be evaluated at every iteration rather than tuned globally. Our approach, on the other hand, avoids this overhead by allowing the learning rate to be tuned once.

5 The Convex Case via Double Momentum

We now turn to the convex setting and provide the first data-dependent guarantees for smooth convex objectives. We further strengthen these results by augmenting our framework with a double-momentum mechanism to enhance robustness to the choice of learning rate. More specifically, we analyze μ2\mu^{2}-SGD (Dahan and Levy, 2025), which is known for its stability under a broad range of step sizes. The μ2\mu^{2}-SGD approach augments standard momentum with two complementary components: (i) a variance-reduction correction term STORM (Cutkosky and Orabona, 2019) that mitigates stochastic gradient noise, and (ii) a parameter-level momentum mechanism, also known as Anytime-SGD (Cutkosky, 2019).

5.1 Assumptions

We establish our results under the following standard assumptions of stochastic convex optimization:

Convexity Under Bounded Diameter: The function f:𝒦→ℝf:\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{R} is convex, where 𝒦⊆d\mathcal{K}\subseteq\real^{d} is a compact convex set, and there exists D>0D>0 such that ∀𝐱,𝐲∈𝒦\forall\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{K}: ‖𝐱−𝐲‖≤D\left\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\right\|\leq D

The bounded diameter assumption means there is a minimum, and we will define 𝐱∗:=arg⁡min𝐱∈𝒦​f​(𝐱)\mathbf{x}^{*}:=\underset{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{K}}{\arg\min}f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right), f∗:=f⁡(𝐱∗)f^{*}:=f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right).

Bounded Variance: There exists σ>0\sigma>0 such that ∀𝐱∈𝒦\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{K}: 𝔼​‖∇f​(𝐱,𝐳)−∇f​(𝐱)‖2≤σ2\mathbb{E}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{z}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)\right\|^{2}\leq\sigma^{2}.

Smoothness: There exist L>0L>0 such that ∀𝐱,𝐲∈𝒦\forall\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{K}: ‖∇f​(𝐱)−∇f​(𝐲)‖≤L⁡‖𝐱−𝐲‖\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{y}\right)\right\|\leq L\left\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\right\|.

Bounded Smoothness Variance (Dahan and Levy, 2025): There exists σL>0\sigma_{L}>0 such that ∀𝐱,𝐲∈𝒦\forall\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{K}: 𝔼​‖(∇f​(𝐱,𝐳)−∇f​(𝐱))−(∇f​(𝐲,𝐳)−∇f​(𝐲))‖2≤σL2​‖𝐱−𝐲‖2\mathbb{E}\left\|\left(\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{z}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)\right)-\left(\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{y};\mathbf{z}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{y}\right)\right)\right\|^{2}\leq\sigma_{L}^{2}\left\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\right\|^{2}.

Notations. For any sequence {an}n\{a_{n}\}_{n}, we use the shorthand ai:j:=∑n=ijana_{i:j}:=\sum_{n=i}^{j}a_{n}, and for every 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, we denote the orthogonal projection of 𝐱\mathbf{x} onto a set 𝒦\mathcal{K} by Π𝒦​(𝐱):=arg⁡min𝐲∈𝒦⁡‖𝐲−𝐱‖2\Pi_{\mathcal{K}}\left(\mathbf{x}\right):=\arg\min_{\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{K}}\left\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\right\|^{2}.

5.2 STOchastic Recursive Momentum (STORM)

One of the momentum components of μ2\mu^{2}-SGD is STORM (Cutkosky and Orabona, 2019), which extends classical momentum (Polyak, 1964) by augmenting the recursion with a sample-reuse correction term:

𝐝tsyn=(1−β)​𝐝t−1syn+β​𝐠t+(1−β)​(𝐠t−𝐠~t−1)⏟correction term\displaystyle\mathbf{d}_{t}^{\text{syn}}=(1-\beta)\mathbf{d}_{t-1}^{\text{syn}}+\beta\mathbf{g}_{t}+\underbrace{(1-\beta)\left(\mathbf{g}_{t}-\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{t-1}\right)}_{\textnormal{correction term}}

where 𝐠t:=∇f​(𝐱t,𝐳t)\mathbf{g}_{t}:=\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t};\mathbf{z}_{t}\right) and 𝐠~t−1:=∇f​(𝐱t−1,𝐳t)\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{t-1}:=\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t-1};\mathbf{z}_{t}\right). Thus, by applying our asynchronous framework to STORM, we derive the ordered asynchronous STORM update:

𝐝t=(1−β)​𝐝t−1+(1−β)τt​(𝐠t−τt−(1−β)​𝐠~t−τt−1)\displaystyle\mathbf{d}_{t}=(1-\beta)\mathbf{d}_{t-1}+(1-\beta)^{\tau_{t}}(\mathbf{g}_{t-\tau_{t}}-(1-\beta)\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{t-\tau_{t}-1}) (12)

This recovers the same momentum term as in Equation 8, along with the STORM correction term, which is likewise ordered according to the correct time index.

Role of the correction.

The STORM correction term exploits objective smoothness to contract stochastic error across successive iterates proportionally to ‖𝐱t−𝐱t−1‖\left\|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\right\| to reduce stochastic error (Cutkosky and Orabona, 2019). While classical momentum stabilizes updates, it introduces a persistent estimator bias, i.e., 𝔼⁡[𝐦tsync]≠∇f​(𝐱t)\mathbb{E}\left[{\mathbf{m}}^{\text{sync}}_{t}\right]\neq\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right). In contrast, STORM introduces a variance-reduction mechanism that ensures the estimator remains unbiased in total expectation, i.e., 𝔼⁡[𝐝tsync]=∇f​(𝐱t)\mathbb{E}\left[{\mathbf{d}}^{\text{sync}}_{t}\right]=\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right), but not conditionally unbiased. Equivalently, we can express this STORM momentum in the simplified recursive form:

𝐝tsyn=𝐠t+(1−β)​(𝐝t−1syn−𝐠~t−1)⏟unbiased term\displaystyle\mathbf{d}_{t}^{\text{syn}}=\mathbf{g}_{t}+\underbrace{(1-\beta)\left(\mathbf{d}_{t-1}^{\text{syn}}-\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{t-1}\right)}_{\textnormal{unbiased term}}

5.3 Anytime-GD

The Anytime-GD mechanism originally proposed by Cutkosky (2019) where the gradient updates the query point directly. It maintains two sequences: the gradient descent iterates {𝐰t}t\{\mathbf{w}_{t}\}_{t} and the averaged parameters {𝐱t}t\{\mathbf{x}_{t}\}_{t}, where 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} is a weighted average of {𝐰τ}τ=1t\{\mathbf{w}_{\tau}\}_{\tau=1}^{t} with positive weights {ατ}τ=1t\{\alpha_{\tau}\}_{\tau=1}^{t}. The updates are given by

𝐰t+1=Π𝒦(𝐰t−ηαt𝐠t),𝐱t+1=𝐱t+αt+1α1:t+1(𝐰t+1−𝐱t)\displaystyle\mathbf{w}_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{K}}\left(\mathbf{w}_{t}-\eta\alpha_{t}\mathbf{g}_{t}\right),\qquad\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\mathbf{x}_{t}+\frac{\alpha_{t+1}}{\alpha_{1:t+1}}\left(\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)

where 𝐠t:=∇f​(𝐱t,𝐳t)\mathbf{g}_{t}:=\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t};\mathbf{z}_{t}\right) is a stochastic gradient computed at the model parameters at iteration t>0t>0. A key property of Anytime-GD is that by applying momentum at the parameter level, it contracts the distance between successive iterates for 𝒦\mathcal{K} with diameter D>0D>0:

‖𝐱t+1−𝐱t‖≤αt+1α1:t+1D\displaystyle\left\|\mathbf{x}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\|\leq\frac{\alpha_{t+1}}{\alpha_{1:t+1}}D

This contraction provides additional stability, and when combined with STORM, it leads to a significant reduction in stochastic variance and improved robustness, as demonstrated by Dahan and Levy (2025).

Under asynchronous convex settings, Aviv et al. (2021) showed that this mechanism adapts the delays by using

𝐰t+1=Π𝒦(𝐰t−ηαt𝐠t−τt),𝐱t+1=𝐱t+αt+1α1:t+1(𝐰t+1−𝐱t)\displaystyle\mathbf{w}_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{K}}\left(\mathbf{w}_{t}-\eta\alpha_{t}\mathbf{g}_{t-\tau_{t}}\right),\qquad\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\mathbf{x}_{t}+\frac{\alpha_{t+1}}{\alpha_{1:t+1}}\left(\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)

with αt=t\alpha_{t}=t. However, their guarantees rely on a data-independence assumption. In contrast, by replacing the SGD estimator with STORM within our asynchronous momentum framework, we obtain optimal convergence guarantees that remain valid even when the data distribution and delay are dependent.

5.4 Combining Anytime and STORM

The combination of Anytime-SGD and STORM proceeds by replacing the stochastic gradient in the Anytime update with the STORM momentum estimator:

𝐰t+1=Π𝒦(𝐰t−ηαt𝐝tsync),𝐱t+1=𝐱t+αt+1α1:t+1(𝐰t+1−𝐱t)\displaystyle\mathbf{w}_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{K}}\left(\mathbf{w}_{t}-\eta\alpha_{t}{\mathbf{d}}^{\text{sync}}_{t}\right),\qquad\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\mathbf{x}_{t}+\frac{\alpha_{t+1}}{\alpha_{1:t+1}}\left(\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)

We use increasing importance weights {αt}t≥1\{\alpha_{t}\}_{t\geq 1} and setting α0=0\alpha_{0}=0. For our analysis, we use a time-varying momentum parameter βt=1−αt−1αt\beta_{t}=1-\frac{\alpha_{t-1}}{\alpha_{t}}. With this choice, the ideal STORM step can be written compactly as:

αt​𝐝tsyn=αt−1​𝐝t−1syn+αt​𝐠t−αt−1​𝐠~t−1\displaystyle\alpha_{t}\mathbf{d}_{t}^{\text{syn}}=\alpha_{t-1}\mathbf{d}_{t-1}^{\text{syn}}+\alpha_{t}\mathbf{g}_{t}-\alpha_{t-1}\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{t-1}

We can unroll this equality and get:

𝐝tsyn=∑k=1t(αkαt​𝐠k−αk−1αt​𝐠~k−1)\displaystyle\mathbf{d}_{t}^{\text{syn}}=\sum_{k=1}^{t}\left(\frac{\alpha_{k}}{\alpha_{t}}\mathbf{g}_{k}-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{\alpha_{t}}\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{k-1}\right)

Note that αkαt=∏m=k+1t(1−βm)\frac{\alpha_{k}}{\alpha_{t}}=\prod_{m=k+1}^{t}(1-\beta_{m}), which makes it analogous to Equation 7. This formulation naturally accommodates non-constant momentum parameters βt\beta_{t}.

For the asynchronous ordered method, we introduce the momentum increment:

𝐬t:=αt​𝐠t−αt−1​𝐠~t−1\displaystyle\mathbf{s}_{t}:=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{g}_{t}-\alpha_{t-1}\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{t-1}

With this definition, the ordered STORM momentum with a varying momentum parameter admits the compact form:

αt​𝐝t=αt−1​𝐝t−1+𝐬t−τt\displaystyle\alpha_{t}\mathbf{d}_{t}=\alpha_{t-1}\mathbf{d}_{t-1}+\mathbf{s}_{t-\tau_{t}} (13)

In general, 𝐝tsync\mathbf{d}^{\text{sync}}_{t} is an unbiased estimator of ∇f​(𝐱t)\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right) (Cutkosky and Orabona, 2019). In the asynchronous setting, 𝐬t\mathbf{s}_{t} is replaced by a delayed increment 𝐬t−τt\mathbf{s}_{t-\tau_{t}} (Equation 13), which introduces bias into the estimator. As discussed earlier, the magnitude of the bias of αt​𝐝t\alpha_{t}\mathbf{d}_{t} scales as 𝒪⁡(M)\mathcal{O}\left(M\right) (see Section 4.2), which means that the bias of 𝐝t\mathbf{d}_{t} is 𝒪⁡(Mt)\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{M}{t}\right).

Theorem 5.1 (Convex Smooth Objectives).

Let ff satisfy the assumptions in Section 5.1. Consider {𝐱t}t=1T\{\mathbf{x}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} to be the iterates generated by the update rule according to Algorithm 2 with αt=t\alpha_{t}=t, where η\eta satisfies:

4​L≤1T​η≤𝒪⁡((σD+σL)​T+L​M)\displaystyle 4L\leq\frac{1}{T\eta}\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\left(\frac{\sigma}{D}+\sigma_{L}\right)\sqrt{T}+LM\right)

Then we get an excess loss bound of:

𝔼​f​(𝐱t)−f∗≤𝒪⁡(D​σ+D2​σLT+D2​L​MT)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-f^{*}\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{D\sigma+D^{2}\sigma_{L}}{\sqrt{T}}+\frac{D^{2}LM}{T}\right)
Remark 5.2.

Optimality under data-dependent delays. We provide the first convergence guarantees for smooth convex objectives under data-dependent delays. Previously, results in this regime were restricted to non-smooth with GG-bounded gradient objectives and suffered a 𝒪⁡(M)\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{M}\right) slowdown in the dominant convergence term 𝒪⁡(D​G​MT)\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{DG\sqrt{M}}{\sqrt{T}}\right) (Mishchenko et al., 2022). In contrast, our analysis shows that for smooth objectives, the dependence on MM is confined to the fast-vanishing term 𝒪⁡(D2​L​MT)\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{D^{2}LM}{T}\right). This aligns with the best-known bounds for data-independent delays (Aviv et al., 2021; Cohen et al., 2021), demonstrating that our framework effectively mitigates the impact of data-dependent delays.

Remark 5.3.

Generality to Data-Dependent Delays. As discussed in Theorem 4.1, our analysis applies to general smooth objectives without assuming independence between the data and the delays, thereby more accurately capturing the dynamics of asynchronous settings.

Remark 5.4.

Practical Learning Rate and Hyperparameter Tuning. Theorem 5.1 shows that μ2\mu^{2}-SGD allows a broad range of learning rates. Specifically, the convergence guarantee holds for any η∈[ηmin,ηmax]\eta\in[\eta_{\min},\eta_{\max}], as long as ηmaxηmin=Θ⁡(T+M)\frac{\eta_{\max}}{\eta_{\min}}=\Theta\left(\sqrt{T}+M\right). Therefore, even under asynchronous updates with data-dependent delays, μ2\mu^{2}-SGD remains stable over this wide range of choices. This flexibility reduces the need for careful hyperparameter tuning and demonstrates robustness to highly variable asynchrony.

Remark 5.5.

The iteration complexities in Theorems 4.1 and 5.1 can be translated into time complexity via the framework of Tyurin and Richtárik (2023). While such optimal-time setups are typically defined for worker-dependent delays, our framework is the first to achieve optimal iteration complexity under general data-dependent delays. Furthermore, by adopting a naive subset-selection strategy that selects the fastest workers (see e.g., Maranjyan et al. (2025)), our method simultaneously recovers optimal time-complexity bounds for worker-dependent delays, ensuring it remains optimal regardless of the delay source.

6 Conclusions and Future Work

This work introduces a momentum-based framework for asynchronous optimization with data-dependent delays. We provide the first convergence guarantees in both convex and non-convex settings without requiring a restrictive delay-independence assumption. By decoupling the convergence analysis from specific delay distributions, our results remain applicable to real-world systems where data and delays are inherently coupled. For future work, a natural next step is to extend our framework to adaptive optimizers such as Adam, AdamW, and related variants. Specifically, analyzing how data-dependent delays interact with the second-moment estimation in adaptive methods could yield more robust asynchronous training for large-scale training.

Appendix A Non-Convex Analysis

Virtual Momentum.

In the spirit of Mishchenko et al. [2022], Shi et al. [2024], we define the virtual momentum 𝐦^t\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{t} (Equation 10), in which all updates are applied exactly at their designated iterations.

Lemma A.1.

let f:d→f:\real^{d}\to\real be a function that satisfies the assumptions in Section 4.1, then for any 𝐱∈d\mathbf{x}\in\real^{d} we have:

‖∇f​(𝐱)‖2≤2​L​(f⁡(𝐱)−f∗)\displaystyle\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)\right\|^{2}\leq 2L\left(f(\mathbf{x})-f^{*}\right)
Proof of Lemma A.1.

By LL-smoothness, for all 𝐱,𝐲∈d\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\real^{d}:

f⁡(𝐲)−f⁡(𝐱)≤⟨∇f​(𝐱),𝐲−𝐱⟩+L2​‖𝐲−𝐱‖2=−12​L​‖∇f​(𝐱)‖2\displaystyle f\!\left(\mathbf{y}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)\leq\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right),\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\left\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\right\|^{2}=-\frac{1}{2L}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)\right\|^{2}

Where we get the equality by setting 𝐲=𝐱−1L∇f(𝐱)\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{x}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right). Using f⁡(𝐲)≥f∗f(\mathbf{y})\geq f^{*} and a simple rearrangement yields the claim. ∎

The use of this lemma is to bound ‖∇f​(𝐱1)‖2≤2​L​Δ\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{1}\right)\right\|^{2}\leq 2L\Delta.

Lemma A.2.

Let f:d→f:\real^{d}\to\real be a function that satisfies the assumptions in Section 4.1. Then, for any iteration t≥1t\geq 1 with momentum parameter β≤116​(M−1)\beta\leq\frac{1}{16(M-1)}, the cumulative stochastic error of the delayed momentum in Algorithm 1, ϵt:=𝐦t−∇f​(𝐱t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}:=\mathbf{m}_{t}-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right), evaluated over TT iterations, satisfies:

1T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖ϵt‖2≤2T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖ϵ^t‖2+14​T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖∇f​(𝐱t)‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{2}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\frac{1}{4T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\right\|^{2}
Proof of Lemma A.2.

We will define the delay 𝐛t:=𝐦t−𝐦^t=ϵt−ϵ^t\mathbf{b}_{t}:=\mathbf{m}_{t}-\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{t}=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}, and note Equation 11:

𝐛t=−∑k∈𝒯⁡(t)𝐠¯t,k\displaystyle\mathbf{b}_{t}=-\sum_{k\in\mathcal{T}(t)}\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t,k}

Next, we use the decomposition ϵt=ϵ^t+𝐛t\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}+\mathbf{b}_{t} and the inequality ‖𝐱+𝐲‖2≤2​‖𝐱‖2+2​‖𝐲‖2\left\|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\right\|^{2}\leq 2\left\|\mathbf{x}\right\|^{2}+2\left\|\mathbf{y}\right\|^{2}, we obtain 𝔼​‖ϵ‖2≤2​𝔼​‖ϵ^t‖2+2​𝔼​‖𝐛t‖2\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right\|^{2}\leq 2\mathbb{E}\left\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}+2\mathbb{E}\left\|\mathbf{b}_{t}\right\|^{2}.

‖𝐛t‖2=‖−∑k∈𝒯⁡(t)𝐠¯t,k‖2≤(M−1)∑k∈𝒯⁡(t)‖𝐠¯t,k‖2\displaystyle\left\|\mathbf{b}_{t}\right\|^{2}=\left\|-\sum_{k\in\mathcal{T}(t)}\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t,k}\right\|^{2}\leq(M-1)\sum_{k\in\mathcal{T}(t)}\left\|\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t,k}\right\|^{2}
≤\displaystyle\leq (M−1)​β2​∑k=1t(1−β)2​(t−k)​‖∇f​(𝐱k)‖2≤β8​∑k=1t(1−β)2​(t−k)​‖∇f​(𝐱k)‖2\displaystyle(M-1)\beta^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{t}(1-\beta)^{2(t-k)}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{k}\right)\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{\beta}{8}\sum_{k=1}^{t}(1-\beta)^{2(t-k)}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{k}\right)\right\|^{2}

Where the first inequality uses Jensen’s inequality and the fact that |𝒯⁡(t)|≤M−1|\mathcal{T}(t)|\leq M-1. In the next inequality we input the definitions of 𝐠¯t,k\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t,k} and add the missing members in the sum. At last, we use the bound (M−1)​β≤116(M-1)\beta\leq\frac{1}{16}.

Averaging the above over TT iterations gives:

1T​∑t=1T‖𝐛t‖2≤\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|\mathbf{b}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq β8​T​∑t=1T∑k=1t(1−β)2​(t−k)​‖∇f​(𝐱k)‖2\displaystyle\frac{\beta}{8T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{k=1}^{t}(1-\beta)^{2(t-k)}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{k}\right)\right\|^{2}
≤\displaystyle\leq β8​T​∑k=1T‖∇f​(𝐱k)‖2​∑t=kT(1−β)2​(t−k)≤18​T​∑k=1T‖∇f​(𝐱k)‖2\displaystyle\frac{\beta}{8T}\sum_{k=1}^{T}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{k}\right)\right\|^{2}\sum_{t=k}^{T}(1-\beta)^{2(t-k)}\leq\frac{1}{8T}\sum_{k=1}^{T}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{k}\right)\right\|^{2}

Where in the last inequality we bound the geometric sum with 1β\frac{1}{\beta}.

Putting it together, we get:

1T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖ϵt‖2≤2T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖ϵ^t‖2+14​T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖∇f​(𝐱t)‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{2}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\frac{1}{4T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\right\|^{2}

∎

Stochastic Variance of the Virtual Momentum.

Following Lemma A.2, we need to bound the error of the virutal momentum.

Lemma A.3.

Let f:d→f:\real^{d}\to\real be a function that satisfies the assumptions in Section 4.1. Then, for any iteration t≥1t\geq 1 with momentum parameter β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), the cumulative stochastic error of the virtual momentum in Algorithm 1, evaluated over TT iterations, satisfies:

1T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖ϵ^t‖2≤2​L​Δβ​T+β​σ2+L2​η2β2​T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖𝐦t‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{2L\Delta}{\beta T}+\beta\sigma^{2}+\frac{L^{2}\eta^{2}}{\beta^{2}T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}
Proof of Lemma A.3.

Using Equation 10, we know that the virtual stochastic error is:

ϵ^t:=𝐦^t−∇f​(𝐱t)=∑k∈[t]/𝒯⁡(t)𝐠t,k+∑k∈𝒯⁡(t)𝐠¯t,k−∇f​(𝐱t)\displaystyle\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}:=\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{t}-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)=\sum_{k\in[t]/\mathcal{T}(t)}\mathbf{g}_{t,k}+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{T}(t)}\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t,k}-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)

We will define the expected stochastic error as:

ϵ¯t=∑k=1t𝐠¯t,k−∇f​(𝐱t)\displaystyle\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}=\sum_{k=1}^{t}\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t,k}-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)

We can tell that 𝔼⁡[ϵ^t−ϵ¯t]=0\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}-\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right]=0 and thus 𝔼​‖ϵ^t‖2=𝔼​‖ϵ^t−ϵ¯t‖2+𝔼​‖ϵ¯t‖2\mathbb{E}\left\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}=\mathbb{E}\left\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}-\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\mathbb{E}\left\|\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}.

𝔼​‖ϵ^t−ϵ¯t‖2=𝔼​‖∑k∈[t]/𝒯⁡(t)(𝐠t,k−𝐠¯t,k)‖2=∑k∈[t]/𝒯⁡(t)𝔼​‖𝐠t,k−𝐠¯t,k‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}-\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}=\mathbb{E}\left\|\sum_{k\in[t]/\mathcal{T}(t)}\left(\mathbf{g}_{t,k}-\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t,k}\right)\right\|^{2}=\sum_{k\in[t]/\mathcal{T}(t)}\mathbb{E}\left\|\mathbf{g}_{t,k}-\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t,k}\right\|^{2}
≤\displaystyle\leq ∑k=1tβ2​(1−β)2​(t−k)​𝔼​‖𝐠k−∇f​(𝐱k)‖2≤β2​σ2​∑k=1t(1−β)2​(t−k)≤β​σ2\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{t}\beta^{2}(1-\beta)^{2(t-k)}\mathbb{E}\left\|\mathbf{g}_{k}-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{k}\right)\right\|^{2}\leq\beta^{2}\sigma^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{t}(1-\beta)^{2(t-k)}\leq\beta\sigma^{2}

Where we used the fact that the sum is a martingale sequence, in the first inequality we added all the missing terms to the sum, then used the bounded variance, and finally bounded the geometric sum.

To bound the expected error we will find its update step:

ϵ¯t=\displaystyle\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}= ∑k=1t𝐠¯t,k−∇f(𝐱t)=(1−β)∑k=1t−1𝐠¯t−1,k−(1−β)∇f(𝐱t)\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{t}\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t,k}-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)=(1-\beta)\sum_{k=1}^{t-1}\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t-1,k}-(1-\beta)\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)
=\displaystyle= (1−β)​(ϵ¯t−1+∇f​(𝐱t−1)−∇f​(𝐱t))\displaystyle(1-\beta)\left(\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t-1}+\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\right)

Where we used 𝐠¯t,t=β∇f(𝐱t)\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t,t}=\beta\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right) and 𝐠¯t,k=(1−β)​𝐠¯t−1,k\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t,k}=(1-\beta)\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t-1,k}. Using this update rule, we get:

‖ϵ¯t+1‖2=\displaystyle\left\|\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t+1}\right\|^{2}= (1−β)2​‖ϵ¯t+∇f​(𝐱t)−∇f​(𝐱t+1)‖2≤(1−β)​‖ϵ¯t‖2+(1−β)2β​‖∇f​(𝐱t)−∇f​(𝐱t+1)‖2\displaystyle(1-\beta)^{2}\left\|\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}+\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right)\right\|^{2}\leq(1-\beta)\left\|\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\frac{(1-\beta)^{2}}{\beta}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right)\right\|^{2}
≤\displaystyle\leq (1−β)​‖ϵ¯t‖2+(1−β)2​L2β​‖𝐱t−𝐱t+1‖2≤(1−β)​‖ϵ¯t‖2+L2​η2β​‖𝐦t‖2\displaystyle(1-\beta)\left\|\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\frac{(1-\beta)^{2}L^{2}}{\beta}\left\|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right\|^{2}\leq(1-\beta)\left\|\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\frac{L^{2}\eta^{2}}{\beta}\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}

Where we used the inequality ‖𝐱+𝐲‖2≤1p‖𝐱‖2+11−p‖𝐲‖2,∀𝐱,𝐲∈d,p∈(0,1)\left\|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{1}{p}\left\|\mathbf{x}\right\|^{2}+\frac{1}{1-p}\left\|\mathbf{y}\right\|^{2},\forall\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\real^{d},p\in(0,1), with p=βp=\beta, the smoothness of ff, and the update rule 𝐱t+1=𝐱t−η​𝐦t\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\mathbf{x}_{t}-\eta\mathbf{m}_{t}. Rearranging the terms and summing over from 1 to T−1T-1 yields:

‖ϵ¯T‖2−‖ϵ¯1‖2+β​∑t=1T−1‖ϵ¯t‖2≤L2​η2β​∑t=1T−1‖𝐦t‖2\displaystyle\left\|\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{T}\right\|^{2}-\left\|\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{1}\right\|^{2}+\beta\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left\|\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{L^{2}\eta^{2}}{\beta}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}

Since ϵ¯1=−(1−β)∇f(𝐱1)\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{1}=-(1-\beta)\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{1}\right), we get:

β​∑t=1T‖ϵ¯t‖2≤\displaystyle\beta\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq (1−β)2​‖∇f​(𝐱1)‖2−(1−β)​‖ϵ¯T‖2+L2​η2β​∑t=1T−1‖𝐦t‖2≤2​L​Δ+L2​η2β​∑t=1T−1‖𝐦t‖2\displaystyle(1-\beta)^{2}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{1}\right)\right\|^{2}-(1-\beta)\left\|\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{T}\right\|^{2}+\frac{L^{2}\eta^{2}}{\beta}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq 2L\Delta+\frac{L^{2}\eta^{2}}{\beta}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}

Dividing by β​T\beta T:

1T​∑t=1T‖ϵ¯t‖2≤2​L​Δβ​T+L2​η2β2​T​∑t=1T−1‖𝐦t‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{2L\Delta}{\beta T}+\frac{L^{2}\eta^{2}}{\beta^{2}T}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}

In total, the virtual error is bounded by:

1T​∑t=1T‖ϵ^t‖2≤2​L​Δβ​T+β​σ2+L2​η2β2​T​∑t=1T‖𝐦t‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{2L\Delta}{\beta T}+\beta\sigma^{2}+\frac{L^{2}\eta^{2}}{\beta^{2}T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}

∎

We will now bound the momentum:

Lemma A.4.

Let f:d→f:\real^{d}\to\real be a function that satisfies the assumptions in Section 4.1, and define the stochastic error as ϵt:=𝐦t−∇f​(𝐱t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}:=\mathbf{m}_{t}-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right). Consider the update rule 𝐱t+1:=𝐱t−η​𝐦t\mathbf{x}_{t+1}:=\mathbf{x}_{t}-\eta\mathbf{m}_{t} with a learning rate η≤12​L\eta\leq\frac{1}{2L}, then:

1T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖𝐦t‖2≤4​Δη​T+2T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖ϵt‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{4\Delta}{\eta T}+\frac{2}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}
Proof of Lemma A.4.

By the smoothness property of ff, it follows since,

f⁡(𝐱t+1)−f⁡(𝐱t)≤\displaystyle f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\leq ⟨∇f​(𝐱t),𝐱t+1−𝐱t⟩+L2​‖𝐱t+1−𝐱t‖2=−η⁡⟨∇f​(𝐱t),𝐦t⟩+L​η22​‖𝐦t‖2\displaystyle\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right),\mathbf{x}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\left\|\mathbf{x}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\|^{2}=-\eta\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right),\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\rangle+\frac{L\eta^{2}}{2}\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}
=\displaystyle= −η​‖𝐦t‖2+η⁡⟨ϵt,𝐦t⟩+L​η22​‖𝐦t‖2≤−η​‖𝐦t‖2+η2​‖ϵt‖2+η2​‖𝐦t‖2+L​η22​‖𝐦t‖2\displaystyle-\eta\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\eta\left\langle\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t},\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\rangle+\frac{L\eta^{2}}{2}\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq-\eta\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\frac{\eta}{2}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\frac{\eta}{2}\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\frac{L\eta^{2}}{2}\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}
≤\displaystyle\leq −η4​‖𝐦t‖2+η2​‖ϵt‖2\displaystyle-\frac{\eta}{4}\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\frac{\eta}{2}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}

Here, the first equality employs the definition of the update rule for 𝐱t+1\mathbf{x}_{t+1} with learning rate η\eta, and the second follows the definition of the stochastic error ϵt:=𝐦t−∇f​(𝐱t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}:=\mathbf{m}_{t}-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right). The next inequality uses the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality ⟨𝐚,𝐛⟩≤12‖𝐚‖2+12‖𝐛‖2,∀𝐚,𝐛∈d\left\langle\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\right\rangle\leq\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathbf{a}\right\|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathbf{b}\right\|^{2},\forall\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\in\real^{d} and the last inequality holds by setting η≤12​L\eta\leq\frac{1}{2L}.

Rearranging the above, we obtain:

‖𝐦t‖2≤4​f⁡(𝐱t)−f⁡(𝐱t+1)η+2​‖ϵt‖2\displaystyle\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq 4\frac{f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right)}{\eta}+2\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}

Averaging over all TT iterations and taking the expectation gives us:

1T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖𝐦t‖2≤4η​T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[f⁡(𝐱t)−f⁡(𝐱t+1)]+2T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖ϵt‖2≤4​Δη​T+2T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖ϵt‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{4}{\eta T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right)\right]+\frac{2}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{4\Delta}{\eta T}+\frac{2}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}

∎

A similar bound we be used for the gradients:

Lemma A.5.

Let f:d→f:\real^{d}\to\real be a function that satisfies the assumptions in Section 4.1, and define the stochastic error as ϵt:=𝐦t−∇f​(𝐱t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}:=\mathbf{m}_{t}-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right). Consider the update rule 𝐱t+1:=𝐱t−η​𝐦t\mathbf{x}_{t+1}:=\mathbf{x}_{t}-\eta\mathbf{m}_{t} with a learning rate η≤1L\eta\leq\frac{1}{L}, then:

1T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖∇f​(𝐱t)‖2≤2​Δη​T+1T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖ϵt‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{2\Delta}{\eta T}+\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}
Proof of Lemma A.5.

By the smoothness property of ff, it follows since,

f⁡(𝐱t+1)−f⁡(𝐱t)≤\displaystyle f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\leq ⟨∇f​(𝐱t),𝐱t+1−𝐱t⟩+L2​‖𝐱t+1−𝐱t‖2\displaystyle\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right),\mathbf{x}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\left\|\mathbf{x}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\|^{2}
=\displaystyle= −η⁡⟨∇f​(𝐱t),∇f​(𝐱t)+ϵt⟩+L​η22​‖∇f​(𝐱t)+ϵt‖2\displaystyle-\eta\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right),\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\rangle+\frac{L\eta^{2}}{2}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}

≤\displaystyle\leq η2​(((1−L​η)−(2−L​η))​‖∇f​(𝐱t)‖2+((1−L​η)+L​η)​‖ϵ‖2)\displaystyle\frac{\eta}{2}\left(((1-L\eta)-(2-L\eta))\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\right\|^{2}+((1-L\eta)+L\eta)\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right\|^{2}\right)
=\displaystyle= −η2​‖∇f​(𝐱t)‖2+η2​‖ϵt‖2\displaystyle-\frac{\eta}{2}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\right\|^{2}+\frac{\eta}{2}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}

Here, the first equality employs the definition of the update rule for 𝐱t+1\mathbf{x}_{t+1} with learning rate η\eta, and the second follows the definition of the stochastic error ϵt:=𝐦t−∇f​(𝐱t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}:=\mathbf{m}_{t}-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right). Rearranging the above, we obtain:

‖∇f​(𝐱t)‖2≤2​f⁡(𝐱t)−f⁡(𝐱t+1)η+‖ϵt‖2\displaystyle\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\right\|^{2}\leq 2\frac{f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right)}{\eta}+\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}

Averaging over all TT iterations and taking the expectation gives us:

1T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖∇f​(𝐱t)‖2≤2η​T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[f⁡(𝐱t)−f⁡(𝐱t+1)]+1T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖ϵt‖2≤2​Δη​T+1T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖ϵt‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{2}{\eta T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right)\right]+\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{2\Delta}{\eta T}+\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}

∎

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

Combining the results of all the previous lemmas gives the following:

1T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖ϵt‖2≤2T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖ϵ^t‖2+14​T​∑t=1T𝔼​‖∇f​(𝐱t)‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{2}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\frac{1}{4T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\right\|^{2}

Appendix B Convex Analysis

For our analysis we will define 𝐪t:=αt​𝐝t\mathbf{q}_{t}:=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{d}_{t}, ϵt:=𝐪t−αt∇f(𝐱t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}:=\mathbf{q}_{t}-\alpha_{t}\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right). We will also use G∗:=∇f​(𝐱∗)G^{*}:=\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right).

We will use these following theorem and lemmas for our bound:

Theorem B.1 (Cutkosky [2019]).

Let f:𝒦→f:\mathcal{K}\to\real be a convex function. Also let {αt>0}t\{\alpha_{t}>0\}_{t} and {𝐰t∈𝒦}t\{\mathbf{w}_{t}\in\mathcal{K}\}_{t}. Let {𝐱t}\{\mathbf{x}_{t}\} be the {ατ}τ=1t\{\alpha_{\tau}\}_{\tau=1}^{t} weighted average of {𝐰τ}τ=1t\{\mathbf{w}_{\tau}\}_{\tau=1}^{t}, meaning: α1:t𝐱t=∑τ=1tατ𝐰τ\alpha_{1:t}\mathbf{x}_{t}=\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\alpha_{\tau}\mathbf{w}_{\tau}. Then the following holds for all t≥1,x∈𝒦t\geq 1,x\in\mathcal{K}:

α1:t(f(𝐱t)−f(𝐱))≤∑τ=1tατ⟨∇f(𝐱τ),𝐰τ−𝐱⟩\displaystyle\alpha_{1:t}(f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right))\leq\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\alpha_{\tau}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle

Concretely, the theorem implies that the excess loss of the weighted average 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} can be related to the weighted regret ∑τ=1tατ​⟨∇f​(𝐱τ),𝐰τ−𝐱⟩\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\alpha_{\tau}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle.

Proof of Theorem B.1.

We will prove by induction.

Induction Basis: For t=1t=1, we get that:

α1​(f⁡(𝐱1)−∇f​(𝐱))≤α1​⟨∇f​(𝐱1),𝐱1−𝐱⟩=α1​⟨∇f​(𝐱1),𝐰1−𝐱⟩\displaystyle\alpha_{1}(f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{1}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right))\leq\alpha_{1}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{1}\right),\mathbf{x}_{1}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle=\alpha_{1}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{1}\right),\mathbf{w}_{1}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle

Where the inequality is the convexity of ff, and the equality is because 𝐰1=𝐱1\mathbf{w}_{1}=\mathbf{x}_{1}.

Induction Assumption: We will assume that Theorem B.1 hold true for some t≥1t\geq 1, meaning:

α1:t(f(𝐱t)−f(𝐱))≤∑τ=1tατ⟨∇f(𝐱τ),𝐰τ−𝐱⟩\displaystyle\alpha_{1:t}(f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right))\leq\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\alpha_{\tau}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle

Induction Step: We will prove for t+1t+1.

α1:t+1(f(𝐱t+1)−f(𝐱))=α1:t(f(𝐱t)−f(𝐱))+α1:t(f(𝐱t+1)−f(𝐱t))+αt+1(f(𝐱t+1)−f(𝐱))\displaystyle\alpha_{1:t+1}(f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right))=\alpha_{1:t}(f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right))+\alpha_{1:t}(f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right))+\alpha_{t+1}(f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right))

We got this by adding and subtracting α1:tf(𝐱t)\alpha_{1:t}f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right). The first term can be bounded by the induction assumption, and the second and third step will each be bounded using the convexity of ff.

α1:t+1(f(𝐱t+1)−f(𝐱))=∑τ=1tατ⟨∇f(𝐱τ),𝐰τ−𝐱⟩+α1:t⟨∇f(𝐱t+1),𝐱t+1−𝐱t⟩+αt+1⟨∇f(𝐱t+1),𝐱t+1−𝐱⟩\displaystyle\alpha_{1:t+1}(f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right))=\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\alpha_{\tau}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle+\alpha_{1:t}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right),\mathbf{x}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\rangle+\alpha_{t+1}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right),\mathbf{x}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle

Combining the last two terms, we get:

α1:t⟨∇f(𝐱t+1),𝐱t+1−𝐱t⟩+αt+1⟨∇f(𝐱t+1),𝐱t+1−𝐱⟩\displaystyle\alpha_{1:t}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right),\mathbf{x}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}_{t}\right\rangle+\alpha_{t+1}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right),\mathbf{x}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle
=\displaystyle= ⟨∇f(𝐱t+1),α1:t+1𝐱t+1−α1:t𝐱t−αt+1𝐱⟩=αt+1⟨∇f(𝐱t+1),𝐰t+1−𝐱⟩\displaystyle\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right),\alpha_{1:t+1}\mathbf{x}_{t+1}-\alpha_{1:t}\mathbf{x}_{t}-\alpha_{t+1}\mathbf{x}\right\rangle=\alpha_{t+1}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\right),\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle

Where in the last term we used α1:t+1𝐱t+1−α1:t𝐱t=αt+1𝐰t+1\alpha_{1:t+1}\mathbf{x}_{t+1}-\alpha_{1:t}\mathbf{x}_{t}=\alpha_{t+1}\mathbf{w}_{t+1}. In total, we got:

α1:t+1(f(𝐱t+1)−f(𝐱))≤∑τ=1t+1ατ⟨∇f(𝐱τ),𝐰τ−𝐱⟩\displaystyle\alpha_{1:t+1}(f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}+1\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right))\leq\sum_{\tau=1}^{t+1}\alpha_{\tau}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle

We proved the induction step. ∎

Lemma B.2.

Let η>0\eta>0, and 𝒦⊂d\mathcal{K}\subset\real^{d} be a convex domain of bounded diameter DD, also let {𝐪t∈d}t=1T\{\mathbf{q}_{t}\in\real^{d}\}_{t=1}^{T} be a sequence of arbitrary vectors. Then for any starting point 𝐰1∈d\mathbf{w}_{1}\in\real^{d}, and an update rule 𝐰t+1=Π𝒦​(wt−η​𝐪t),∀t≥1\mathbf{w}_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{K}}\left(w_{t}-\eta\mathbf{q}_{t}\right),~\forall t\geq 1, the following holds ∀𝐱∈𝒦\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{K}:

∑τ=1t⟨𝐪τ,𝐰τ+1−𝐱⟩≤D22​η−12​η​∑τ=1t‖𝐰τ−𝐰τ+1‖2\displaystyle\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\left\langle\mathbf{q}_{\tau},\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle\leq\frac{D^{2}}{2\eta}-\frac{1}{2\eta}\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\left\|\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\|^{2}
Proof of Lemma B.2.

The update rule 𝐰t+1=Π𝒦​(𝐰t−η​𝐪t)\mathbf{w}_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{K}}\left(\mathbf{w}_{t}-\eta\mathbf{q}_{t}\right) can be re-written as a convex optimization problem over 𝒦\mathcal{K}:

wt+1=Π𝒦​(𝐰t−η​𝐪t)=arg⁡min𝐱∈𝒦​{‖𝐰t−η​𝐪t−𝐱‖2}=arg⁡min𝐱∈𝒦​{⟨𝐪t,𝐱−𝐰t⟩+12​η​‖𝐱−𝐰t‖2}\displaystyle w_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{K}}\left(\mathbf{w}_{t}-\eta\mathbf{q}_{t}\right)=\underset{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{K}}{\arg\min}\left\{\left\|\mathbf{w}_{t}-\eta\mathbf{q}_{t}-\mathbf{x}\right\|^{2}\right\}=\underset{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{K}}{\arg\min}\left\{\left\langle\mathbf{q}_{t},\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{w}_{t}\right\rangle+\frac{1}{2\eta}\left\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{w}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right\}

The first equality is our update definition, the second is by the definition of the projection operator, and then we rewrite it in a way that does not affect the minimum point.

Now, since 𝐰t+1\mathbf{w}_{t+1} is the minimal point of the above convex problem, then from optimality conditions we obtain:

⟨𝐪t+1η​(wt+1−𝐰t),𝐱−𝐰t+1⟩≥0,∀x∈𝒦\displaystyle\left\langle\mathbf{q}_{t}+\frac{1}{\eta}(w_{t+1}-\mathbf{w}_{t}),\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{w}_{t+1}\right\rangle\geq 0,\quad\forall x\in\mathcal{K}

Re-arranging the above, we get that:

⟨𝐪t,𝐰t+1−𝐱⟩≤1η​⟨𝐰t−𝐰t+1,𝐰t+1−𝐱⟩=12​η​‖𝐰t−𝐱‖2−12​η​‖𝐰t+1−𝐱‖2−12​η​‖𝐰t−𝐰t+1‖2\displaystyle\left\langle\mathbf{q}_{t},\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle\leq\frac{1}{\eta}\left\langle\mathbf{w}_{t}-\mathbf{w}_{t+1},\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle=\frac{1}{2\eta}\left\|\mathbf{w}_{t}-\mathbf{x}\right\|^{2}-\frac{1}{2\eta}\left\|\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}\right\|^{2}-\frac{1}{2\eta}\left\|\mathbf{w}_{t}-\mathbf{w}_{t+1}\right\|^{2}

Where the equality is an algebraic manipulation. After summing over tt we get:

∑τ=1t⟨𝐪τ,𝐰τ+1−𝐱⟩≤12​η​∑τ=1t(‖𝐰τ−𝐱‖2−‖𝐰τ+1−𝐱‖2−‖𝐰τ−𝐰τ+1‖2)\displaystyle\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\left\langle\mathbf{q}_{\tau},\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle\leq\frac{1}{2\eta}\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\left(\left\|\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{x}\right\|^{2}-\left\|\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}-\mathbf{x}\right\|^{2}-\left\|\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\|^{2}\right)
=‖𝐰1−𝐱‖2−‖𝐰t+1−𝐱‖22​η−12​η​∑τ=1t‖𝐰τ−𝐰τ+1‖2≤D22​η−12​η​∑τ=1t‖𝐰τ−𝐰τ+1‖2\displaystyle=\frac{\left\|\mathbf{w}_{1}-\mathbf{x}\right\|^{2}-\left\|\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}\right\|^{2}}{2\eta}-\frac{1}{2\eta}\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\left\|\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{D^{2}}{2\eta}-\frac{1}{2\eta}\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\left\|\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\|^{2}

Where the second line is due to splitting the sum into two sums, and using the fact that the first one is a telescopic sum, and lastly, we use the diameter of 𝒦\mathcal{K}. This establishes the lemma. ∎

Lemma B.3.

If f:𝒦→f:\mathcal{K}\to\real is convex and LL-smooth, and 𝐱∗=arg⁡min𝐱∈𝒦​f​(𝐱)\mathbf{x}^{*}=\underset{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{K}}{\arg\min}f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right), then ∀𝐱∈𝒦\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{K}:

‖∇f​(𝐱)−∇f​(𝐱∗)‖2≤2​L​(f⁡(𝐱)−f⁡(𝐱∗))\displaystyle\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right)\right\|^{2}\leq 2L(f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right))
Proof of Lemma B.3.

Let us define a new function:

h⁡(𝐱)=f⁡(𝐱)−f⁡(𝐱∗)−⟨∇f​(𝐱∗),𝐱−𝐱∗⟩\displaystyle h(\mathbf{x})=f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right)-\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right),\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{*}\right\rangle

Since ff is convex and LL-smooth, we know that:

0≤h⁡(𝐱)≤L2​‖𝐱−𝐱∗‖2\displaystyle 0\leq h(\mathbf{x})\leq\frac{L}{2}\left\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{*}\right\|^{2}

The gradient of this function is:

∇h​(𝐱)=∇f​(𝐱)−∇f​(𝐱∗)\displaystyle\nabla h(\mathbf{x})=\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right)

We can see that h⁡(𝐱∗)=0,∇h​(𝐱∗)=0h(\mathbf{x}^{*})=0,\nabla h(\mathbf{x}^{*})=0, and that x∗x^{*} is the global minimum. The function hh is also convex and LL-smooth, since the gradient is the same as ff up to a constant translation. We will add to the domain of hh to include all d, while still being convex and LL-smooth. Since hh is convex then:

h(𝐲)≥h(𝐱∗)+⟨∇h(𝐱∗),y−𝐱∗⟩=0,∀y∈d\displaystyle h(\mathbf{y})\geq h(\mathbf{x}^{*})+\left\langle\nabla h(\mathbf{x}^{*}),y-\mathbf{x}^{*}\right\rangle=0,\quad\forall y\in\real^{d}

It is true even for points outside of the original domain, meaning that 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*} remains the global minimum even after this. For a smooth function, ∀𝐱,𝐲∈d\forall\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\real^{d}:

h⁡(𝐲)≤h⁡(𝐱)+⟨∇h​(𝐱),𝐲−𝐱⟩+L2​‖𝐲−𝐱‖2\displaystyle h(\mathbf{y})\leq h(\mathbf{x})+\left\langle\nabla h(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\left\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\right\|^{2}

By picking 𝐲=𝐱−1L∇h(𝐱)\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{x}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla h(\mathbf{x}), we get:

h⁡(𝐱)−h⁡(𝐲)≥12​L​‖∇h​(𝐱)‖2\displaystyle h(\mathbf{x})-h(\mathbf{y})\geq\frac{1}{2L}\left\|\nabla h(\mathbf{x})\right\|^{2}

Rearranging, we get:

‖∇h​(𝐱)‖2≤2​L​(h⁡(𝐱)−h⁡(𝐲))≤2​L⋅h⁡(𝐱)\displaystyle\left\|\nabla h(\mathbf{x})\right\|^{2}\leq 2L(h(\mathbf{x})-h(\mathbf{y}))\leq 2L\cdot h(\mathbf{x})

By using 𝐱∈𝒦\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{K} we get:

‖∇f​(𝐱)−∇f​(𝐱∗)‖2≤2​L​(f⁡(𝐱)−f⁡(𝐱∗)−⟨∇f​(𝐱∗),𝐱−𝐱∗⟩)\displaystyle\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right)\right\|^{2}\leq 2L\left(f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right)-\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right),\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{*}\right\rangle\right)

Since 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*} is the minimum point of ff then:

⟨∇f​(𝐱∗),𝐱−𝐱∗⟩≥0,∀𝐱∈𝒦\displaystyle\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right),\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{*}\right\rangle\geq 0,\quad\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{K}

Thus we get that:

‖∇f​(𝐱)−∇f​(𝐱∗)‖2≤2​L​(f⁡(𝐱)−f⁡(𝐱∗))\displaystyle\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right)\right\|^{2}\leq 2L(f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right))

∎

These two lemmas will help us bound the excess loss for an Anytime algorithm.

Lemma B.4.

Let f:𝒦→f:\mathcal{K}\to\real be a convex and smooth function with smoothness parameter L>0L>0, and define the stochastic error as ϵt:=αt​(𝐝t−∇f​(𝐱t))\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}:=\alpha_{t}(\mathbf{d}_{t}-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)). Consider the Anytime-GD update rule 𝐰t+1:=Π𝒦(𝐰t−ηαt𝐝t),𝐱t+1=𝐱t+αt+1α1:t+1(𝐰t+1−𝐱t)\mathbf{w}_{t+1}:=\Pi_{\mathcal{K}}\left(\mathbf{w}_{t}-\eta\alpha_{t}\mathbf{d}_{t}\right),\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\mathbf{x}_{t}+\frac{\alpha_{t+1}}{\alpha_{1:t+1}}(\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{x}_{t}) with {αt=t}t=1T\{\alpha_{t}=t\}_{t=1}^{T} and learning rate η≤14​L​T\eta\leq\frac{1}{4LT}, then:

𝔼⁡[f⁡(𝐱T)]−f⁡(𝐱∗)≤2​D2η​T2+4​D​G∗T+4​DT2​∑t=1T𝔼​‖ϵt‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{T}\right)\right]-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right)\leq\frac{2D^{2}}{\eta T^{2}}+\frac{4DG^{*}}{T}+\frac{4D}{T^{2}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}}

Where 𝐱∗:=arg⁡min𝐱∈𝒦​f​(𝐱)\mathbf{x}^{*}:=\underset{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{K}}{\arg\min}f\!\left(\mathbf{x}\right), and G∗:=∇f​(𝐱∗)G^{*}:=\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right).

Proof of Lemma B.4.

We will define the excess loss at time tt as Δt:=𝔼⁡[f⁡(𝐱T)]−f⁡(𝐱∗)\Delta_{t}:=\mathbb{E}\left[f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{T}\right)\right]-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right), and follow a similar analysis as in Reshef and Levy [2024], Reshef and Levy [2025]. Start by bounding the excess loss:

α1:tΔt:=\displaystyle\alpha_{1:t}\Delta_{t}:= α1:t(𝔼[f(𝐱t)]−f(𝐱∗))≤∑τ=1tατ𝔼⟨∇f(𝐱τ),𝐰τ−𝐱∗⟩\displaystyle\alpha_{1:t}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)\right]-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right)\right)\leq\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\alpha_{\tau}\mathbb{E}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{x}^{*}\right\rangle
=\displaystyle= ∑τ=1tατ​𝔼​⟨∇f​(𝐱τ),𝐰τ+1−𝐱∗⟩+∑τ=1tατ​𝔼​⟨∇f​(𝐱τ),𝐰τ−𝐰τ+1⟩\displaystyle\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\alpha_{\tau}\mathbb{E}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}-\mathbf{x}^{*}\right\rangle+\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\alpha_{\tau}\mathbb{E}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\rangle
=\displaystyle= ∑τ=1t𝔼⁡⟨𝐪τ,𝐰τ+1−𝐱∗⟩+∑τ=1t𝔼⁡⟨ϵτ,𝐱∗−𝐰τ+1⟩+∑τ=1tατ​𝔼​⟨∇f​(𝐱τ),𝐰τ−𝐰τ+1⟩\displaystyle\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}\left\langle\mathbf{q}_{\tau},\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}-\mathbf{x}^{*}\right\rangle+\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}\left\langle\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\tau},\mathbf{x}^{*}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\rangle+\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\alpha_{\tau}\mathbb{E}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\rangle
≤\displaystyle\leq D22​η−12​η​∑τ=1t𝔼​‖𝐰τ−𝐰τ+1‖2+∑τ=1t𝔼⁡⟨ϵτ,𝐱∗−𝐰τ+1⟩+∑τ=1tατ​𝔼​⟨∇f​(𝐱τ),𝐰τ−𝐰τ+1⟩\displaystyle\frac{D^{2}}{2\eta}-\frac{1}{2\eta}\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}\left\|\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\|^{2}+\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}\left\langle\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\tau},\mathbf{x}^{*}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\rangle+\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\alpha_{\tau}\mathbb{E}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\rangle
≤\displaystyle\leq D22​η+∑τ=1t(ατ​𝔼​⟨∇f​(𝐱τ)−∇f​(𝐱∗),𝐰τ−𝐰τ+1⟩−12​η​‖𝐰τ−𝐰τ+1‖2)\displaystyle\frac{D^{2}}{2\eta}+\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\left(\alpha_{\tau}\mathbb{E}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\rangle-\frac{1}{2\eta}\left\|\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\|^{2}\right)
+\displaystyle+ ∑τ=1t𝔼⟨ατ∇f(𝐱∗),𝐰τ−𝐰τ+1⟩+∑τ=1t𝔼⟨ϵτ,𝐱∗−𝐰τ+1⟩\displaystyle\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}\left\langle\alpha_{\tau}\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\rangle+\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}\left\langle\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\tau},\mathbf{x}^{*}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\rangle

The first sum can be bounded as such:

ατ​𝔼​⟨∇f​(𝐱τ)−∇f​(𝐱∗),𝐰τ−𝐰τ+1⟩−12​η​𝔼​‖𝐰τ−𝐰τ+1‖2\displaystyle\alpha_{\tau}\mathbb{E}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\rangle-\frac{1}{2\eta}\mathbb{E}\left\|\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\|^{2}
≤\displaystyle\leq η2ατ2𝔼‖∇f(𝐱τ)−∇f(𝐱∗)‖2≤2Lηα1:τ𝔼[f(𝐱τ)−f(𝐱∗)]=2Lηα1:τΔτ\displaystyle\frac{\eta}{2}\alpha_{\tau}^{2}\mathbb{E}\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}\right)-\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right)\right\|^{2}\leq 2L\eta\alpha_{1:\tau}\mathbb{E}\left[f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}\right)-f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right)\right]=2L\eta\alpha_{1:\tau}\Delta_{\tau}

Where at first we used Young’s inequality, and then we bound ατ2≤2α1:τ\alpha_{\tau}^{2}\leq 2\alpha_{1:\tau} and use Lemma B.3.

For the second sum, we do this:

∑τ=1t𝔼⟨ατ∇f(𝐱∗),𝐰τ−𝐰τ+1⟩=∑τ=1t(ατ−ατ−1)𝔼⟨∇f(𝐱∗),𝐰τ⟩−αt𝔼⟨∇f(𝐱∗),𝐰t+1⟩\displaystyle\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}\left\langle\alpha_{\tau}\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\rangle=\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}(\alpha_{\tau}-\alpha_{\tau-1})\mathbb{E}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau}\right\rangle-\alpha_{t}\mathbb{E}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right),\mathbf{w}_{t+1}\right\rangle
=\displaystyle= ∑τ=1t(ατ−ατ−1)​𝔼​⟨∇f​(𝐱∗),𝐰τ−𝐰t+1⟩≤∑τ=1t(ατ−ατ−1)​‖∇f​(𝐱∗)‖​𝔼​[‖𝐰τ−𝐰t+1‖]\displaystyle\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}(\alpha_{\tau}-\alpha_{\tau-1})\mathbb{E}\left\langle\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right),\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{t+1}\right\rangle\leq\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}(\alpha_{\tau}-\alpha_{\tau-1})\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right)\right\|\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{w}_{\tau}-\mathbf{w}_{t+1}\right\|\right]
≤\displaystyle\leq D⁡‖∇f​(𝐱∗)‖​∑τ=1t(ατ−ατ−1)=αt​D​‖∇f​(𝐱∗)‖=αt​D​G∗\displaystyle D\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right)\right\|\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}(\alpha_{\tau}-\alpha_{\tau-1})=\alpha_{t}D\left\|\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{*}\right)\right\|=\alpha_{t}DG^{*}

The first equality is rearrangement of the sum while defining α0=0\alpha_{0}=0, then we put the last term into the sum, and use Cauchy-Schwartz, and finally, we use the diameter bound and telescope the sum.

For the third sum we just use Cauchy-Schwartz:

𝔼⁡⟨ϵτ,𝐱∗−𝐰τ+1⟩≤𝔼​‖ϵτ‖2​𝔼​‖𝐱∗−𝐰τ+1‖2≤D​𝔼​‖ϵτ‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left\langle\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\tau},\mathbf{x}^{*}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\rangle\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\tau}\right\|^{2}}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left\|\mathbf{x}^{*}-\mathbf{w}_{\tau+1}\right\|^{2}}\leq D\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\tau}\right\|^{2}}

In total, we get:

α1:tΔt≤2Lη∑τ=1tα1:τΔτ+D22​η+αtDG∗+D∑τ=1t𝔼​‖ϵτ‖2\displaystyle\alpha_{1:t}\Delta_{t}\leq 2L\eta\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\alpha_{1:\tau}\Delta_{\tau}+\frac{D^{2}}{2\eta}+\alpha_{t}DG^{*}+D\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\tau}\right\|^{2}}

Notice that if η≤14​L​T\eta\leq\frac{1}{4LT}, we get that:

α1:tΔt≤\displaystyle\alpha_{1:t}\Delta_{t}\leq 12​T∑τ=1tα1:τΔτ+D22​η+αtDG∗+D∑τ=1t𝔼​‖ϵτ‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{2T}\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\alpha_{1:\tau}\Delta_{\tau}+\frac{D^{2}}{2\eta}+\alpha_{t}DG^{*}+D\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\tau}\right\|^{2}}
≤\displaystyle\leq 12​T∑τ=1Tα1:τΔτ+D22​η+αTDG∗+D∑τ=1T𝔼​‖ϵτ‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{2T}\sum_{\tau=1}^{T}\alpha_{1:\tau}\Delta_{\tau}+\frac{D^{2}}{2\eta}+\alpha_{T}DG^{*}+D\sum_{\tau=1}^{T}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\tau}\right\|^{2}}

α1:TΔT≤D2η+2αTDG∗+2D∑τ=1T𝔼​‖ϵτ‖2\displaystyle\alpha_{1:T}\Delta_{T}\leq\frac{D^{2}}{\eta}+2\alpha_{T}DG^{*}+2D\sum_{\tau=1}^{T}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\tau}\right\|^{2}}

since α1:T≥T22\alpha_{1:T}\geq\frac{T^{2}}{2}, we get:

ΔT≤2​D2η​T2+4​D​G∗T+4​DT2​∑t=1T𝔼​‖ϵt‖2\displaystyle\Delta_{T}\leq\frac{2D^{2}}{\eta T^{2}}+\frac{4DG^{*}}{T}+\frac{4D}{T^{2}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\right\|^{2}}

∎

Note that this part in the bound is only reliant on the Anytime-GD mechanism.

Now we just need to bound ϵt\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}. We will define these momentum increments: 𝐬^t:=αt−τt​𝐠t−τt−αt−τt−1​𝐠t−τt−1\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{t}:=\alpha_{t-\tau_{t}}\mathbf{g}_{t-\tau_{t}}-\alpha_{t-\tau_{t}-1}\mathbf{g}_{t-\tau_{t}-1} is the momentum increment given at iteration tt, 𝐬t:=αt​𝐠t−αt−1​𝐠t−1\mathbf{s}_{t}:=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{g}_{t}-\alpha_{t-1}\mathbf{g}_{t-1} is the momentum calculated in iteration tt, with the special case of 𝐬1(i):=α1​𝐠1(i)\mathbf{s}_{1}^{(i)}:=\alpha_{1}\mathbf{g}_{1}^{(i)}, and 𝐬¯t:=αt∇f(𝐱t)−αt−1∇f(𝐱t−1)\bar{\mathbf{s}}_{t}:=\alpha_{t}\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\right)-\alpha_{t-1}\nabla f\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\right) is the expected momentum at iteration tt. We also define α0=0\alpha_{0}=0.

𝒯⁡(t)\mathcal{T}(t) is the group of missing iterations at time tt, as in the non-convex analysis. We will also define I⁡(t)I(t) to be the group of all machines that had at least one turn up to time tt, and i⁡(t)i(t) will be the machine that played at time tt. Note that I⁡(t)={i⁡(t)}∨{i⁡(k)|k∈𝒯⁡(t)}I(t)=\{i(t)\}\vee\{i(k)|k\in\mathcal{T}(t)\}. We can look at the weighted momentum 𝐪t\mathbf{q}_{t} in a new way:
